summary: Defines SIP extensions that let a caller express preferences about how a request is handled by servers. These include choosing which contact URIs the request is routed to and giving directives such as whether to try several places at once or one after another.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 3841 lets the person making a call add instructions to the request. The caller can say do not fork the request, or try all the addresses at once, and can also describe the kind of phone it wants to reach, for example a mobile device rather than a desk phone.

Those instructions travel in three new SIP header fields. A proxy reads them, compares them with what it knows about each of the callee's devices, and drops or reorders the list of addresses accordingly.

questions: what does accept-contact do in sip
what is the sip request-disposition header
how does a sip proxy rank contacts
subtitle: Letting a SIP caller say which of a callee's devices it wants to reach, and how.

tldr.problem: A SIP server decides many things when it routes a request: whether to proxy or redirect, which addresses to try, whether to try them at once or in turn. The server administrator controls some of these, and the callee controls others, but the caller had no way to state a preference at all.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3841 defines three request header fields. Request-Disposition carries directives about how the request should be processed, such as fork or no-fork. Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact carry feature sets describing the kind of user agent the caller wants or does not want to reach.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from August 2004 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It also warns that preferences change how a request is handled, so requests carrying them should be integrity protected, and that a server should reject a request with an unreasonable number of rules.

facts.label: Compact header forms
facts.value: a for Accept-Contact, j for Reject-Contact, d for Request-Disposition

today: RFC 3841 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2004. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the three SIP header fields that carry caller preferences and of the matching rules proxies apply.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When a SIP server receives a request there are a number of decisions it can make regarding the processing of the request: whether to proxy or redirect the request, which URIs to proxy or redirect to, whether to fork or not, whether to search recursively or not, and whether to search in parallel or sequentially. The server can base these decisions on any local policy, which can be statically configured, or based on the execution of a program or a database access.

The administrator of the server is not the only entity with an interest in request processing. There are at least three parties: the administrator of the server, the user who sent the request, and the user to whom the request is directed. The directives of the administrator are embedded in the policy of the server, and the preferences of the user to whom the request is directed can be expressed most easily through a script written in a scripting language such as the Call Processing Language. No mechanism existed to incorporate the preferences of the user who sent the request. For example, the caller might want to speak to a specific user but wants to reach them only at work, because the call is a business call; or the caller might want to reach a user but not their voicemail, since it is important that the caller talk to the called party.

The extension allows the caller to have these preferences met by specifying mechanisms by which a caller can provide preferences on the processing of a request. There are two types. The first, called request handling preferences, are encapsulated in the Request-Disposition header field and provide specific request handling directives for a server. The second, called feature preferences, is present in the Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact header fields, which allow the caller to provide a feature set that expresses its preferences on the characteristics of the user agent that is to be reached. These are matched with a feature set provided by a user agent to its registrar. The extension is very general purpose and not tied to a particular service; it is a tool that can be used in the development of many services.

One example of a service enabled by caller preferences is a one-number service. A user can have a single identity, their SIP URI, for all of their devices, such as a cell phone, a PDA, a work phone and a home phone. If the caller wants to reach the user at their business phone, they simply select business phone from a pull-down menu when calling that URI, and users no longer need to maintain and distribute separate identities for each device.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP servers make several routing decisions on every call. Today only the server operator and the person being called have a say in them. This document gives the caller a say as well.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.content:
The document defines several terms. A caller refers to the user on whose behalf a user agent is operating; it is not limited to a user whose user agent sends an INVITE request. Feature preferences are caller preferences that describe desired properties of a user agent to which the request is to be routed, and can be made explicit with the Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact header fields. Request handling preferences are caller preferences that describe desired request treatment at a server, and are carried in the Request-Disposition header field.

A target set is a set of candidate URIs to which a proxy or redirect server can send or redirect a request. Frequently, target sets are obtained from a registration, but they need not be. An explicit preference is a caller preference indicated explicitly in the Accept-Contact or Reject-Contact header fields. An implicit preference is a caller preference implied through the presence of other aspects of a request; for example, if the request method is INVITE, it represents an implicit caller preference to route the request to a user agent that supports the INVITE method.

When a caller sends a request, it can optionally include new header fields which request certain handling at a server. The first category, request handling preferences, is carried in the Request-Disposition header field and describes specific behaviour that is desired at a server, including whether the caller wishes the server to proxy or redirect, and whether sequential or parallel search is desired. These preferences can be applied at every proxy or redirect server on the call signalling path.

The second category, feature preferences, is carried in the Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact header fields. These header fields contain feature sets, represented by the same feature parameters that are used to indicate capabilities. The Accept-Contact header field contains feature sets that describe user agents the caller would like to reach. The Reject-Contact header field contains feature sets which, if matched by a user agent, imply that the request should not be routed to that agent.

Proxies use the information in the Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact header fields to select amongst contacts in their target set. When neither of those header fields is present, the proxy computes implicit preferences from the request, which are not explicitly placed into the request but can be inferred from the presence of other message components. Both kinds of preference can appear in any request, not just INVITE, but they are only useful in requests where proxies need to determine a request target. If the domain in the request URI is not owned by any proxies along the request path, those proxies will never access a location service and so will never have the opportunity to apply the caller preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: The document draws a line between two kinds of instruction. One kind tells the server how to handle the request, such as whether to try several addresses at once. The other kind describes the device the caller wants to reach.

sections.title: UAC Behavior
sections.content:
A caller wishing to express preferences for a request includes Accept-Contact, Reject-Contact or Request-Disposition header fields in the request, depending on their particular preferences. No additional behavior is required after the request is sent. The Accept-Contact, Reject-Contact and Request-Disposition header fields in an ACK for a non-2xx final response, or in a CANCEL request, must be equal to the values in the original request being acknowledged or cancelled, so that the request works properly through stateless proxies.

If the user agent wants to determine whether servers along the path understand the header fields, it includes a Proxy-Require header field with a value of pref in its request. If the request should fail with a 420 response code, the user agent knows that the extension is not supported, and in that case it should retry and may decide whether or not to use caller preferences. A user agent should only use Proxy-Require if knowledge about support is essential. Caller preferences can only be considered preferences: there is no guarantee that the requested service will be executed.

The Request-Disposition header field specifies caller preferences for how a server should process a request. Its value is a list of tokens, each of which specifies a particular processing directive.

A user agent can also indicate preferences for the capabilities of a user agent that should be reached or not reached. It does that by adding one or more Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact header field values, each of which contains a set of feature parameters that define a feature set. The feature sets placed into these header fields may overlap. It is recommended that a user agent include a term in an Accept-Contact feature set with the sip.methods feature tag whose value includes the method of the request, and, when it sends a SUBSCRIBE request, a term with the sip.events feature tag whose value includes the event package of the request. As an example, the Accept-Contact header field *;mobility="mobile";methods="INVITE" expresses a desire to route a call to a mobile device.

The Reject-Contact header field allows the user agent to specify that a user agent should not be contacted if it matches any of the values of the header field. Each value contains a '*', purely to align the syntax with the guidelines for SIP extensions, and is parameterized by a set of feature parameters. Any user agent whose capabilities match the feature set described by the feature parameters matches the value.

The behaviour of Accept-Contact depends heavily on whether the require and explicit parameters are present. When both are present, a proxy will only forward the request to contacts which have explicitly indicated that they support the desired feature set, and any others are discarded. A user agent should only use require and explicit together when it wishes the call to fail unless a contact definitively matches; a user agent might support a desired feature but not have indicated it in its registration, and such a contact would not be reached.

When only require is present, a contact will not be used if it does not match; if it does match, or if it is not known whether it is a complete match, the contact is still used. A user agent would use require alone when a non-matching contact is useless, which is common for services where the request simply cannot be serviced without the necessary features. The proxy will also preferentially route the request to the user agent that represents the best match, meaning the one that has explicitly indicated it supports more of the desired features than any other. This preferential routing never overrides an ordering provided by the called party and only chooses amongst contacts of equal q-value.

When only explicit is present, all contacts provided by the callee will be used, but a contact that is not an explicit match is tried last amongst contacts with the same q-value. The difference from using require and explicit together is the fallback behaviour for contacts that do not match explicitly: here they are tried as a last resort, whereas if require is also present they are never tried.

Finally, if neither require nor explicit is present, all contacts provided by the callee will be used, but a contact that does not match is tried last amongst contacts with the same q-value, and if it does match the request is routed preferentially to the best match. This is a common configuration for preferences that, if not honoured, will still allow a successful call, and the greater the match, the better.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller adds the instructions to the request and then does nothing else. If the caller needs to know whether the servers understand them, it asks for that with a special header and gets a 420 error if they do not.

sections.title: UAS Behavior
sections.content:
When a user agent server compliant with this specification receives a request whose request URI corresponds to one of its registered contacts, it should apply the behaviour described for proxies as if it were a proxy for the domain in the request URI. The user agent acts as if its location database contains a single request target for the request URI, and that target is associated with a feature set, the same one that was placed in the registration of the URI in the request URI. If a user agent had registered against multiple separate addresses-of-record, and the contacts registered for each had different capabilities, it will have used a different URI in each registration, so it can determine which feature set to use.

This processing occurs after the client authenticates and authorizes the request, but before the remainder of the general user agent server processing described in RFC 3261. If, after performing this processing, there are no URIs left in the target set, the user agent should reject the request with a 480 response. If a URI remains, the user agent proceeds with request processing as per RFC 3261.

Having a user agent server perform the matching operations as if it were a proxy allows certain caller preferences to be honoured even if the proxy does not support the extension. A user agent server should process any queue directive present in a Request-Disposition header field in the request; all other directives must be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The device that answers the call also does the matching, using the capabilities it registered with. That way the caller's instructions still work even when the proxy in between does not understand them.

sections.title: Proxy Matching
sections.content:
Proxy behaviour consists of two orthogonal sets of rules, one for processing the Request-Disposition header field and one for processing the URI and feature set preferences in the Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact header fields. A proxy may add one of these header fields if it is not present, or add a value to an existing header field, as if it were a user agent, which is useful for requesting processing in downstream proxies. However, a proxy must not modify or remove an existing header field value. This is particularly important when S/MIME is used, because the message signature could include the caller preferences header fields, allowing the user agent server to verify that the original caller preferences were still present.

A proxy must not apply the preferences matching operation to a request unless it is the owner of the domain in the request URI and is accessing a location service that has capabilities associated with request targets. If it is, it should apply the processing. Typically this is a proxy using a registration database to determine the request targets, but if a proxy knows about capabilities through some other means it should apply the processing as well. The processing is described through a conversion from the syntax of this specification to RFC 2533 syntax, followed by a matching operation and a sorting of the resulting contact values. The use of RFC 2533 syntax as an intermediate step is not required; it only serves as a useful tool to describe the required behaviour, and a proxy can use any steps it likes as long as the results are identical.

The first step is to extract explicit preferences, looking for the Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact header fields. For each value of those header fields, the proxy extracts the feature parameters, which are the header field parameters whose name is audio, automata, class, duplex, data, control, mobility, description, events, priority, methods, extensions, schemes, application, video, language, type, isfocus, actor or text, or whose name begins with a plus sign. The proxy converts all of those parameters to RFC 2533 syntax. The result is a set of feature set predicates in conjunctive normal form, each associated with one of the two preference header fields. If there was a require parameter associated with a header field value in Accept-Contact, the derived predicate has its require flag set; similarly for the explicit parameter and its explicit flag.

If, and only if, the proxy found no explicit preferences in the request, it extracts implicit preferences. First it creates a conjunction with no terms, representing a feature set that will be associated with the Accept-Contact header field as if it were included there. This feature set has its require flag set but not its explicit flag. The proxy then adds a term for the method, of the form (sip.methods=[method of request]), because a request with a specific method is an implicit preference to have the request routed only to user agents that support that method. For requests that establish a subscription, the Event header field is another expression of an implicit preference, adding a term of the form (sip.events=[value of the Event header field]).

The proxy then takes each URI in the target set and obtains its capabilities as an RFC 2533 formatted feature set predicate, called a contact predicate. If the target URI was obtained through a registration, the proxy computes the contact predicate by extracting the feature parameters from the Contact header field and converting them. It creates an initial empty list of feature parameters, copies in any of the recognised parameters, and copies in any parameter whose name begins with a plus sign if the list does not already contain that name with the plus removed.

If the URI in the target set had no feature parameters, it is said to be immune to caller preference processing: the URI is removed from the target set temporarily, the caller preferences processing is executed, and then the URI is added back in. The resulting predicate is associated with a q-value. If the contact predicate was learned through a REGISTER request, the q-value is equal to the q-value in the Contact header field parameter, otherwise 1.0.

The proxy does not have to know anything about the meaning of the feature tags it compares. The rules depend on syntactic hints in the values: a predicate such as (foo>=4) implies that the feature tag foo is a numeric value. Quoted strings are matched case-sensitively, tokens case-insensitively, and the two are differentiated by the presence of angle brackets around the feature tag value. Numerics are matched using normal mathematical comparisons.

First the proxy applies the predicates associated with the Reject-Contact header field. For each contact predicate, each Reject-Contact predicate is examined. If the Reject-Contact predicate contains a filter for a feature tag that is not present anywhere in the contact predicate, that Reject-Contact predicate is discarded for the processing of that contact predicate. Otherwise it is matched with the contact predicate, and if the result is a match the URI is discarded from the target set. The result is that Reject-Contact will only discard URIs where the user agent has explicitly indicated support for the features that are not wanted.

Next the proxy applies the Accept-Contact predicates. For each contact that remains, the proxy constructs a matching set, initially containing all of the Accept-Contact predicates. Each predicate is matched with the contact predicate. If the result is not a match and the predicate had its require flag set, the URI is discarded. If the result is not a match but the require flag was not set, the contact URI is not discarded, but the Accept-Contact predicate is removed from the matching set for that contact.

For each contact that remains, the proxy computes a score against each predicate in the contact's matching set. If the number of terms in the Accept-Contact predicate conjunction is N, and the contact predicate has a term containing that same feature tag, the score is incremented by 1/N. The score ranges between zero and one. The require and explicit tags are then applied: if the score was less than one, the predicate had an explicit tag, and the predicate also had a require tag, then the contact URI is dropped; if the predicate did not have a require tag, the score is set to zero; if there was no explicit tag, the score is unchanged.

The next step is to combine the scores and the q-values associated with the predicates in the matching set to arrive at an overall caller preference, Qa. If there are M Accept-Contact predicates in the matching set there will be M scores for each contact, and Qa is the arithmetic average of them. Any URIs that were removed because they were immune are added back in, and their Qa is set to 1.0.

The purpose of Qa is to provide an ordering for contacts remaining in the target set if the callee has not provided one. The contacts are sorted by the q-value provided by the callee, grouped into equivalence classes of equal q-value, and within each class ordered by their values of Qa.

If there were no URIs in the target set after the processing, and the caller preferences were based on implicit preferences, the processing is discarded and the original target set, ordered by its original q-values, is used. This handles the case where implicit preferences for the method or event packages resulted in the elimination of all potential targets: by going back to the original target set, those URIs will be tried and will result in a 405 or 489 response, which gives the caller information it can act on. The target set can also be empty after explicit preferences, which results in a 480 from the proxy, and that behaviour is desirable because the caller made an explicit preference and is agreeing that its request might fail.
sections.plainLanguage:
The proxy first throws away any address that matches a Reject-Contact rule. It then checks what is left against the Accept-Contact rules, dropping addresses that break a rule marked as required and scoring the rest on how well they matched.

The score decides the order of the addresses that are left, but only between addresses the callee gave the same priority.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The document gives a contrived but illustrative example. There are five registered contacts for sip:user@example.com: sip:u1@h.example.com with audio, video, methods INVITE and BYE, and a q-value of 0.2; sip:u2@h.example.com with audio FALSE, methods INVITE, actor msg-taker, and a q-value of 0.2; sip:u3@h.example.com with audio, actor msg-taker, methods INVITE, video, and a q-value of 0.3; sip:u4@h.example.com with audio, methods INVITE and OPTIONS, and a q-value of 0.2; and sip:u5@h.example.com with no feature parameters and a q-value of 0.5.

The INVITE contained the preferences Reject-Contact: *;actor="msg-taker";video, Accept-Contact: *;audio;require, Accept-Contact: *;video;explicit and Accept-Contact: *;methods="BYE";class="business";q=1.0. There are no implicit preferences in this example, because explicit preferences are provided.

The proxy first removes u5 from the target set, since it is immune from caller preferences processing. Next it processes the Reject-Contact header field. It matches all four remaining contacts, but only an explicit match for u3, because u3 is the only one that explicitly indicated support for video and explicitly indicated it is a message taker. So u3 is discarded and the others remain.

Next, each of the remaining three contacts is compared against each of the three Accept-Contact predicates. u1 is a match to all three, earning a score of 1.0 for the first two predicates and 0.5 for the third, since the methods feature tag was present in the contact predicate but the class tag was not. u2 does not match the first predicate, and because that predicate has a require tag, u2 is discarded. u4 matches the first predicate, earning a score of 1.0. u4 matches the second predicate, but since the match is not explicit the score is set to zero, which it already was. u4 does not match the third predicate.

At this point u1 and u4 remain. u1 matched all three Accept-Contact predicates, so its matching set contains all three, with scores of 1, 1 and 0.5. u4 matches the first two predicates, with scores of 1.0 and 0.0. Qa for u1 is 0.83 and Qa for u4 is 0.5. u5 is added back in with a Qa of 1.0.

The remaining contacts are then sorted by q-value. u5 has a value of 0.5, and u1 and u4 each have a q-value of 0.2, so there are two equivalence classes. The first, with a q-value of 0.5, consists of just u5. The second has a q-value of 0.2, and within it the two contacts are ordered by their values of Qa, so u1 with a Qa of 0.83 comes before u4 with a Qa of 0.5. The resulting overall ordered set of contacts in the target set is u5, u1 and then u4.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example follows five devices through the rules. One is discarded because it matches the reject rule, one because it fails a required rule, and the two that survive are put in order by how well they matched.

sections.title: The Three Header Fields
sections.content:
The specification defines three new header fields: Accept-Contact, Reject-Contact and Request-Disposition. All three are requests only, and all three may appear in any request method, with the exception that Request-Disposition does not appear in a REGISTER request.

The Request-Disposition header field specifies caller preferences for how a server should process a request. Its value is a list of tokens, each of which specifies a particular directive. A compact form using the letter d has been defined. The directives are grouped into types, and there can only be one directive of each type per request, so a request cannot have both proxy and redirect in the same header field. When the caller specifies a directive, the server should honour it.

The proxy-directive indicates whether the caller would like each server to proxy or redirect. The cancel-directive indicates whether the caller would like each proxy server to send a CANCEL request downstream in response to a 200 OK from the downstream server, which is the normal mode of operation and makes it redundant, or whether this function should be left to the caller. A proxy that receives a request with this parameter set to no-cancel should not cancel any outstanding branches on receipt of a 2xx, but it would still send CANCEL on any outstanding branches on receipt of a 6xx.

The fork-directive indicates whether a proxy should fork a request or proxy to only a single address. If the server is requested not to fork, it should proxy the request to the best address, generally the one with the highest q-value, and if there are multiple addresses with the highest q-value the server chooses one based on its local policy. The directive is ignored if redirect has been requested.

The recurse-directive indicates whether a proxy server receiving a 3xx response should send requests to the addresses listed in the response, or forward the list of addresses upstream towards the caller. The directive is ignored if redirect has been requested. The parallel-directive indicates, for a forking proxy server, whether the caller would like the proxy server to proxy the request to all known addresses at once, or go through them sequentially, contacting the next address only after it has received a non-2xx or non-6xx final response for the previous one. The directive is ignored if redirect has been requested.

The queue-directive applies when the called party is temporarily unreachable, for example because it is in another call. The caller can indicate that it wants the call queued or rejected immediately. If the call is queued the server returns 182 Queued, and a queued call can be terminated as described in RFC 3261. The example given is Request-Disposition: proxy, recurse, parallel. The set of request disposition directives is not extensible on purpose, to avoid a proliferation of new extensions to SIP that are tunnelled through this header field.

For Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact, a compact form has been defined with the letter a and the letter j respectively. Each value of either field contains a '*' and is parameterized by a set of feature parameters. Despite the BNF, there must not be more than one require parameter or explicit parameter in a set of Accept-Contact parameters, and there can only be one instance of any feature tag in a feature parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: Request-Disposition is a list of instructions, one of each kind. Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact each hold a list of descriptions of the kind of device the caller does or does not want.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The presence of caller preferences in a request has an effect on the ways in which the request is handled at a server. As a result, requests with caller preferences should be integrity-protected with the sips mechanism specified in RFC 3261.

Processing of caller preferences requires set operations and searches which can require some amount of computation. This enables a denial of service attack whereby a user can send requests with substantial numbers of caller preferences, in the hopes of overloading the server. To counter this, servers should reject requests with too many rules. A reasonable number is around 20.
sections.plainLanguage: Preferences change what a server does, so an attacker could use them to steer a call somewhere they should not be able to reach. The document says such requests should be signed, and that a server should refuse a request that carries an absurd number of rules.

items.label: proxy-directive
items.desc: Whether the caller would like each server to proxy the request or redirect it.

items.label: cancel-directive
items.desc: Whether each proxy sends a CANCEL downstream on a 200 OK, or leaves that to the caller. A 6xx still triggers CANCEL.

items.label: fork-directive
items.desc: Whether the proxy should fork the request or proxy to only a single address, generally the one with the highest q-value.

items.label: recurse-directive
items.desc: Whether a proxy receiving a 3xx sends requests to the addresses in the response or forwards the list upstream to the caller.

items.label: parallel-directive
items.desc: Whether a forking proxy tries all known addresses at once, or contacts the next one only after a non-2xx or non-6xx final response.

items.label: queue-directive
items.desc: Whether the call is queued when the called party is temporarily unreachable, or rejected immediately. A queued call returns 182 Queued.
